body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Fungi that infect the outside layers of skin or hair are classified as…

A. Cutaneous
B. Subcutaneous
C. Superficial
D. Systemic
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Cutaneous | **F** |
| B. Subcutaneous | **F** |
| C. **Superficial** | **T** |
| D. Systemic | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Superficial mycoses involve only the outermost layers of skin and hair.
hint: Outermost layer only.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Mycoses are grouped by depth: **superficial** (outer stratum corneum and hair surface, e.g. pityriasis versicolor from *Malassezia furfur*, black piedra, tinea nigra — little or no inflammation); **cutaneous** (keratinised skin, hair and nails, the dermatophytes); **subcutaneous** (dermis and subcutaneous tissue after trauma); and **systemic/deep** (internal organs).

## Simplified explanation

Infections of only the **outside layers** of skin and hair are called **superficial**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Fungi that only infect compromised hosts are classified as…

A. Opportunistic
B. Subcutaneous
C. Superficial
D. Systemic
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Opportunistic** | **T** |
| B. Subcutaneous | **F** |
| C. Superficial | **F** |
| D. Systemic | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Fungi causing disease only in compromised hosts are opportunistic.
hint: They need the host's defences to be down.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Opportunistic mycoses** are caused by fungi of low virulence that exploit impaired defences — *Candida*, *Aspergillus*, *Cryptococcus*, *Mucor*/*Rhizopus* and *Pneumocystis*. Risk factors: neutropenia, HIV, steroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, diabetes, catheters and transplantation.

## Simplified explanation

Fungi that only attack people whose defences are weak are **opportunistic**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Fungi that are localized and enter by trauma are classified as…

A. Cutaneous
B. Opportunistic
C. Subcutaneous
D. Superficial
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Cutaneous | **F** |
| B. Opportunistic | **F** |
| C. **Subcutaneous** | **T** |
| D. Superficial | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Subcutaneous mycoses follow traumatic implantation and stay localized.
hint: Implanted through the skin by injury.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Subcutaneous mycoses** follow traumatic inoculation of soil or plant material: **sporotrichosis** (*Sporothrix schenckii*), **chromoblastomycosis**, **mycetoma (eumycetoma)** and **phaeohyphomycosis**. They spread slowly in dermis, subcutis and lymphatics; dissemination is rare.

## Simplified explanation

Fungi pushed under the skin by **injury** cause **subcutaneous** infections.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following are characteristics of histoplasmosis infection:

A. Mycelial phase in the soil
B. Person-to-person transmission
C. Specific geographic distribution
D. Yeasts in tissue
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Mycelial phase in the soil | **T** |
| B. Person-to-person transmission | **F** |
| C. Specific geographic distribution | **T** |
| D. Yeasts in tissue | **T** |

> [!answer]
> A, C and D are true; histoplasmosis is not transmitted from person to person.
hint: A dimorphic fungus acquired from the environment.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Histoplasma capsulatum* is **thermally dimorphic**: a **mould with tuberculate macroconidia** in soil (especially soil enriched with bird or bat droppings) at 25°C, and a small **intracellular yeast** within macrophages at 37°C. Infection follows **inhalation of conidia**; it is endemic in river valleys such as the Ohio and Mississippi and in parts of Africa, and is **not** spread between people.

## Simplified explanation

It grows as a **mould in soil** and a **yeast in the body**, is caught by breathing in spores, and is **not** passed person to person.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following systemic mycosis is endemic to the deserts of the south-western United States:

A. Blastomycosis
B. Coccidioidomycosis
C. Histoplasmosis
D. Paracoccidioidomycosis
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Blastomycosis | **F** |
| B. **Coccidioidomycosis** | **T** |
| C. Histoplasmosis | **F** |
| D. Paracoccidioidomycosis | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Coccidioidomycosis ("Valley fever") is the desert mycosis of the south-western USA.
hint: Valley fever.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Coccidioides immitis*/*posadasii* lives in arid alkaline soil of the south-western USA, Mexico and parts of South America. Arthroconidia are inhaled and form **spherules packed with endospores** in tissue. Blastomycosis occurs around the Great Lakes and Mississippi; paracoccidioidomycosis is South American.

## Simplified explanation

**Coccidioidomycosis** is the desert fungus of the south-western USA.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following is mostly seen in children before puberty:

A. Tinea capitis
B. Tinea corporis
C. Tinea cruris
D. Tinea unguium
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Tinea capitis** | **T** |
| B. Tinea corporis | **F** |
| C. Tinea cruris | **F** |
| D. Tinea unguium | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) is predominantly a disease of pre-pubertal children.
hint: Scalp ringworm.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Tinea capitis** is common in children and usually resolves at puberty, when sebum with fungistatic fatty acids increases. Agents include *Trichophyton* and *Microsporum* species; treatment must be **systemic** (griseofulvin, terbinazole/terbinafine or itraconazole) because topical agents do not reach the hair follicle. Tinea cruris and unguium are commoner in adults.

## Simplified explanation

Scalp ringworm (**tinea capitis**) mostly affects **children**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Aspergillosis is recognized in tissue by the presence of…

A. Budding cells
B. Metachromatic granules
C. Pseudohyphae
D. Septate hyphae
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Budding cells | **F** |
| B. Metachromatic granules | **F** |
| C. Pseudohyphae | **F** |
| D. **Septate hyphae** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> Aspergillus appears in tissue as septate hyphae branching at acute (about 45°) angles.
hint: Compare with the mucormycosis agents.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Aspergillus* shows **septate hyphae with regular dichotomous branching at ~45°**. The **Mucorales** show broad, **aseptate (sparsely septate) ribbon-like hyphae branching at ~90°**. *Candida* shows budding yeasts with **pseudohyphae**; metachromatic (volutin) granules belong to *Corynebacterium*.

## Simplified explanation

Aspergillus in tissue looks like **septate hyphae** branching at a narrow angle.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

A girl who pricked her finger while pruning rose bushes develops a local pustule that progresses to an ulcer. Several nodules then develop along the local lymphatic drainage. The most likely agent is…

A. *Aspergillus fumigatus*
B. *Candida albicans*
C. *Cryptococcus neoformans*
D. *Sporothrix schenckii*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Aspergillus fumigatus* | **F** |
| B. *Candida albicans* | **F** |
| C. *Cryptococcus neoformans* | **F** |
| D. ***Sporothrix schenckii*** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> *Sporothrix schenckii* — classic "rose gardener's disease" with lymphocutaneous spread.
hint: Rose thorn injury with nodules along a lymphatic.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis** follows traumatic implantation of *Sporothrix* from soil, plants or thorns: a papule ulcerates and secondary nodules appear along the draining lymphatics. In tissue the yeasts are **cigar-shaped**; the fungus is **dimorphic**. Treatment is itraconazole (potassium iodide is a traditional alternative).

## Simplified explanation

A **rose-thorn prick** followed by a line of nodules up the arm is **sporotrichosis**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

*Cryptococcus neoformans*:

A. Its budding yeasts are found in the lesions
B. Its natural habitat is the soil, especially associated with pigeon faeces
C. Pathogenesis is related primarily to the production of exotoxin A
D. The initial site of infection is usually the lungs
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Budding yeasts in lesions | **T** |
| B. Soil associated with pigeon faeces | **T** |
| C. Pathogenesis due to exotoxin A | **F** |
| D. Initial site usually the lungs | **T** |

> [!answer]
> A, B and D true; virulence rests on the polysaccharide capsule, not an exotoxin.
hint: What makes this yeast different from other yeasts?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*C. neoformans* is an **encapsulated budding yeast** acquired by **inhalation** from soil enriched with pigeon droppings. Its main virulence factors are the **polysaccharide capsule** (antiphagocytic) and melanin production — not exotoxins. Pulmonary infection is often silent, with later spread to the **meninges**; diagnosis uses India ink, cryptococcal antigen or culture.

## Simplified explanation

It is a **capsuled yeast** from bird droppings, breathed into the **lungs**; its capsule, not a toxin, makes it harmful.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Fungal cells that reproduce by budding are seen in the infected tissues of patients with…

A. Candidiasis, cryptococcosis and sporotrichosis
B. Mycetoma, candidiasis and mucormycosis
C. Sporotrichosis, mycetoma and aspergillosis
D. Tinea corporis, tinea unguium and tinea versicolor
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Candidiasis, cryptococcosis and sporotrichosis** | **T** |
| B. Mycetoma, candidiasis and mucormycosis | **F** |
| C. Sporotrichosis, mycetoma and aspergillosis | **F** |
| D. Tinea corporis, tinea unguium and tinea versicolor | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Only A lists three infections in which budding yeast cells appear in tissue.
hint: Which agents are yeasts in the body?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Candida* (budding yeasts with pseudohyphae), *Cryptococcus* (encapsulated budding yeasts) and *Sporothrix* (cigar-shaped budding yeasts at 37°C) all appear as **yeasts in tissue**. Mycetoma shows grains of filamentous organisms, mucormycosis and aspergillosis show hyphae, and the dermatophytoses show hyphae and arthroconidia. *Malassezia* in tinea versicolor shows yeasts **and** short hyphae ("spaghetti and meatballs").

## Simplified explanation

**Candida, Cryptococcus and Sporothrix** appear as **budding yeasts** in the body.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Infection with a dermatophyte is often associated with…

A. Adherence of the organism to perspiration-moist skin
B. Faecal-oral transmission
C. Inhalation of the organism from contaminated bird faeces
D. Intravenous drug abuse
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Adherence to perspiration-moist skin** | **T** |
| B. Faecal-oral transmission | **F** |
| C. Inhalation from bird faeces | **F** |
| D. Intravenous drug abuse | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Dermatophytes are acquired by contact and favour warm, moist, keratinised skin.
hint: Think of athlete's foot.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Dermatophytes (*Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, *Epidermophyton*) digest **keratin** and spread by direct contact with people (anthropophilic), animals (zoophilic) or soil (geophilic), and by fomites such as towels, floors and shared footwear. **Warmth, moisture and occlusion** favour adherence and invasion. Bird-faeces inhalation suggests *Cryptococcus* or *Histoplasma*.

## Simplified explanation

Ringworm fungi stick to **warm, sweaty skin** and spread by contact.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

*Candida albicans*:

A. Causes thrush
B. Impaired cell-mediated immunity is an important predisposing factor
C. Is a budding yeast that forms pseudohyphae when it invades tissues
D. Is transmitted primarily by respiratory aerosol
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Causes thrush | **T** |
| B. Impaired cell-mediated immunity predisposes | **T** |
| C. Budding yeast forming pseudohyphae in tissue | **T** |
| D. Transmitted primarily by respiratory aerosol | **F** |

> [!answer]
> A, B and C true; *Candida* is endogenous flora, not an aerosol-transmitted organism.
hint: Where does Candida normally live?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*C. albicans* is **normal flora** of mouth, gut and vagina; disease follows disturbance of that balance (antibiotics, steroids, diabetes, pregnancy) or impaired **cell-mediated immunity** (HIV, chemotherapy), which predisposes especially to mucosal candidiasis. In tissue it forms **budding yeasts with pseudohyphae and true hyphae**; germ tube formation is the classical rapid identification test.

## Simplified explanation

Candida lives on us already and causes **thrush** when defences or normal flora are disturbed.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Mycetismus is caused by…

A. Close contact with infected individuals
B. Ingestion of mushrooms
C. Inhalation of fungal allergens
D. Traumatic inoculation of fungi beneath the skin
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Close contact with infected individuals | **F** |
| B. **Ingestion of mushrooms** | **T** |
| C. Inhalation of fungal allergens | **F** |
| D. Traumatic inoculation beneath the skin | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Mycetismus is mushroom poisoning — illness from eating toxic mushrooms.
hint: It is a poisoning, not an infection.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Fungi harm people in four ways: **infection (mycoses)**, **allergy (hypersensitivity)**, **mycotoxicosis** (ingesting toxins formed in food, e.g. aflatoxin) and **mycetismus** (eating poisonous mushrooms, e.g. *Amanita phalloides*). Traumatic inoculation gives subcutaneous mycoses.

## Simplified explanation

Mycetismus means being **poisoned by eating mushrooms**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The fruiting body of a mushroom is called a…

A. Conidiocarp
B. Sorocarp
C. Basidiocarp
D. Ascocarp
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Conidiocarp | **F** |
| B. Sorocarp | **F** |
| C. **Basidiocarp** | **T** |
| D. Ascocarp | **F** |

> [!answer]
> A mushroom's fruiting body is a basidiocarp.
hint: Mushrooms belong to the Basidiomycota.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Mushrooms are **Basidiomycota**, producing sexual **basidiospores** on basidia borne in a **basidiocarp**. **Ascomycota** form ascospores in asci within an **ascocarp**. Sorocarps are formed by cellular slime moulds.

## Simplified explanation

A mushroom cap is a **basidiocarp**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Fungal allergens generally stimulate…

A. Type I hypersensitivity
B. Type II hypersensitivity
C. Type III hypersensitivity
D. Type IV hypersensitivity
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Type I hypersensitivity** | **T** |
| B. Type II hypersensitivity | **F** |
| C. Type III hypersensitivity | **F** (type III does occur in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, but the expected answer is type I) |
| D. Type IV hypersensitivity | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Fungal allergens characteristically provoke immediate, IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity.
hint: Immediate, IgE-mediated reactions.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Inhaled spores of *Aspergillus*, *Alternaria*, *Cladosporium* and *Penicillium* are common aeroallergens causing **type I** rhinitis and asthma. More complex syndromes involve several mechanisms: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis combines type I and **type III**, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer's lung) involves types III and **IV**.

## Simplified explanation

Mould spores usually cause **immediate (type I) allergy** such as asthma and hay fever.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Fungi are important in the production of…

A. Antibiotics
B. Beer
C. Cheese
D. Rubber
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Antibiotics | **T** |
| B. Beer | **T** |
| C. Cheese | **T** |
| D. Rubber | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Fungi are used to make antibiotics, beer and cheese; rubber comes from plants (or is synthesised).
hint: Three of these involve yeasts or moulds.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Beneficial uses of fungi: **penicillin** (*Penicillium chrysogenum*), cephalosporins, griseofulvin, statins, ciclosporin; **brewing and baking** (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*); **cheese ripening** (*Penicillium roqueforti*, *P. camemberti*); soy sauce; citric acid; and recombinant proteins.

## Simplified explanation

Fungi help make **medicines, beer and cheese** — not rubber.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following fungi are most likely to be found within reticuloendothelial cells:

A. *Candida albicans*
B. *Cryptococcus neoformans*
C. *Histoplasma capsulatum*
D. *Sporothrix schenckii*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Candida albicans* | **F** |
| B. *Cryptococcus neoformans* | **F** |
| C. ***Histoplasma capsulatum*** | **T** |
| D. *Sporothrix schenckii* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> *Histoplasma capsulatum* is the intracellular fungus, multiplying inside macrophages.
hint: Which fungus hides inside macrophages?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Inhaled *Histoplasma* conidia are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but **survive and multiply inside them**, spreading through the reticuloendothelial system to liver, spleen and bone marrow. Bone marrow or buffy-coat smears may show small intracellular yeasts; disseminated disease is typical of advanced HIV.

## Simplified explanation

*Histoplasma* grows **inside macrophages**, so it spreads through the body's clearing cells.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Nutritionally, fungi may best be characterized as…

A. Absorptive heterotrophs
B. Chemosynthetic autotrophs
C. Ingestive heterotrophs
D. Photosynthetic autotrophs
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Absorptive heterotrophs** | **T** |
| B. Chemosynthetic autotrophs | **F** |
| C. Ingestive heterotrophs | **F** |
| D. Photosynthetic autotrophs | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Fungi are absorptive heterotrophs: they digest externally and absorb soluble nutrients.
hint: They digest first, then absorb.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Fungi lack chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise, and they do not engulf food as protozoa do. They secrete **exoenzymes** that break down complex substrates outside the cell and then **absorb** the soluble products — the basis of their role as decomposers and of keratin digestion by dermatophytes.

## Simplified explanation

Fungi **digest food outside themselves** and then soak up the nutrients.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Common manifestations of *Cryptococcus* infection in AIDS patients include…

A. Blindness
B. Cutaneous infection
C. Meningitis
D. Pneumonia
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Blindness | **F** |
| B. Cutaneous infection | **F** (as marked; skin lesions do occur in disseminated disease) |
| C. **Meningitis** | **T** |
| D. **Pneumonia** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> Meningitis is the classic presentation, with pneumonia at the site of entry.
hint: Which organ does it reach after the lungs?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Cryptococcal meningitis** is a leading cause of adult meningitis in high-HIV-prevalence settings, presenting subacutely with headache, fever and raised intracranial pressure. Diagnosis: cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) in serum or CSF, India ink, and culture. Treatment: amphotericin B with flucytosine, then fluconazole.

## Simplified explanation

In advanced HIV, *Cryptococcus* typically causes **meningitis**, after entering through the **lungs**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following subcutaneous mycoses may exhibit respiratory and cerebral forms:

A. Chromoblastomycosis
B. Mycetoma
C. Phaeohyphomycosis
D. Sporotrichosis
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Chromoblastomycosis | **F** |
| B. Mycetoma | **F** |
| C. **Phaeohyphomycosis** | **T** |
| D. Sporotrichosis | **F** (as marked; disseminated and pulmonary sporotrichosis can occur in immunocompromised hosts) |

> [!answer]
> Phaeohyphomycosis is the one that characteristically includes respiratory and cerebral forms.
hint: Caused by dematiaceous (dark) fungi.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Phaeohyphomycosis** covers infections by **dematiaceous (melanised) fungi** such as *Cladophialophora bantiana* and *Exophiala*, whose presentations range from subcutaneous cysts to sinusitis, pneumonia and **brain abscess**. Chromoblastomycosis (with sclerotic bodies) and mycetoma (with grains and sinus tracts) stay localized to skin and deeper tissue.

## Simplified explanation

**Phaeohyphomycosis** — caused by dark-walled fungi — can also affect the **lungs and brain**.

body:
(a) All the fungal pathogens that cause systemic mycoses manifest initially as a pulmonary disease. Describe the diagnosis of **any one** of the systemic fungal pathogens a patient may have.

(b) Why are cutaneous mycotic infections usually non-transmissible in the same way?
answer:
**(a) Example — blastomycosis (*Blastomyces dermatitidis*)**

- **Direct microscopy**: a positive diagnosis is made when the fungus is identified by direct microscopic examination of body fluids such as **sputum**, prostatic fluid, pus or tissue from the lungs or skin (KOH or calcofluor preparations; histology with PAS or GMS stains).
- **Morphology in tissue**: yeasts **5–20 µm** in diameter showing **broad-based budding**, **refractile**, with a **double-contoured (thick) cell wall**.
- **Culture**: isolate the fungus from sputum or tissue on Sabouraud dextrose agar — a mould with conidia at 25°C converting to the yeast form at 37°C (**dimorphism**), confirmed by DNA probe or exoantigen test.
- Supporting tests: antigen detection (urine/serum), serology, and chest radiography.

**(b)** Cutaneous (dermatophyte) infections remain in **keratinised, superficial tissue** and the fungus is a **soil/animal saprophyte adapted to keratin** rather than to invasive spread between hosts. Transmission needs **direct contact with infected skin, hair or fomites** plus suitable conditions (warmth, moisture, minor trauma) and host susceptibility, so they do not spread readily as respiratory or systemic infections do.

> [!answer]
> Blastomycosis: direct microscopy of sputum or tissue showing broad-based budding yeasts 5–20 µm with a thick double-contoured wall, plus culture showing dimorphism. Cutaneous mycoses stay in surface keratin and need direct contact, so they do not transmit like deep infections.
hint: Microscopy plus culture; and think where dermatophytes live.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The endemic systemic mycoses — blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis — are all acquired by **inhaling conidia**, so the lung is the primary site, with later dissemination. Each has a characteristic tissue form: broad-based budding yeast (*Blastomyces*), small intracellular yeasts (*Histoplasma*), spherules with endospores (*Coccidioides*), and "mariner's wheel" multiple budding (*Paracoccidioides*).

## Simplified explanation

Diagnose by **looking at sputum or tissue under the microscope and culturing** the fungus. Skin fungi stay in the dead surface layer, so they spread only by close contact.

body:
Traditionally, ringworm is not actually a worm but a fungus. This fungus can be found anywhere on the body, but not usually the scalp, groin, palms or soles. Ringworm may or may not itch, and may even have a burning sensation.

A. What is the epidemiology of this infection?
B. State any **two** symptoms of this mycotic infection.
answer:
**A. Epidemiology (tinea corporis).** It is a **prevalent infection of humans**, appearing nearly anywhere on the body's smooth, bare (glabrous) skin. The principal sources are **other humans, animals and soil**, and it is transmitted primarily by **direct contact and fomites** (towels, clothing, bedding, floors, barbering tools). It is commoner in **warm, humid climates**, with crowding, sharing of personal items, occlusive clothing and sweating as risk factors; it affects all ages.

**B. Symptoms (any two).**
- One or more **scaly, reddish ring-shaped lesions** with a raised, advancing border and central clearing, on the trunk, hip, arm, neck or face.
- **Itching (pruritus)**.
- A **burning sensation**.
- Scaling, and sometimes vesicles or pustules at the active edge.

> [!answer]
> Spread by direct contact and fomites from humans, animals and soil, favoured by heat and humidity; symptoms include an itchy, scaly ring-shaped lesion with central clearing and a burning sensation.
hint: The ring grows outward from where infection started.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The ring pattern forms because the fungus **radiates outward from the original site of invasion** into surrounding skin, with the active, inflamed edge at the periphery. Diagnosis is by KOH microscopy of skin scrapings and culture; treatment is topical azoles or terbinafine (systemic if widespread or follicular).

## Simplified explanation

Ringworm spreads by **touch and shared items**, and makes an **itchy, scaly ring** that spreads outwards.

body:
A 30-year-old woman comes into your laboratory to show you how her skin is changing. She is concerned about the red colour of her chest. You recognize these hyper-pigmented macules as a certain superficial mycosis. When illuminated by a Wood's lamp it fluoresces bright yellow.

A. What is the aetiologic agent of her complaint?
B. What differential diagnosis will you perform on this woman?
answer:
**A.** ***Malassezia furfur*** (*Pityrosporum orbiculare*), causing **pityriasis (tinea) versicolor**.

**B. Differential diagnosis / confirmatory work-up:**
- **Wood's lamp** examination — yellow to golden fluorescence (as seen here).
- **KOH (or calcofluor) microscopy of skin scrapings**, showing the classic **"spaghetti and meatballs"** appearance: short, stubby hyphae with clusters of round yeast cells.
- Culture only if needed, on medium **overlaid with olive oil** (the organism is lipophilic).
- Clinically distinguish from **tinea corporis**, **vitiligo** and **post-inflammatory hypo/hyperpigmentation**, **pityriasis rosea**, **seborrhoeic dermatitis** and **erythrasma** (coral-red fluorescence, *Corynebacterium minutissimum*).

> [!answer]
> *Malassezia furfur* causing pityriasis versicolor; confirm with Wood's lamp and KOH microscopy showing "spaghetti and meatballs", and distinguish from vitiligo, tinea corporis and erythrasma.
hint: Patchy pigment change on the chest that fluoresces.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Malassezia* is **lipophilic normal skin flora** that overgrows in heat, humidity and oily skin, producing azelaic acid, which inhibits melanocytes and gives hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches. Treatment: topical selenium sulfide, ketoconazole shampoo or topical azoles; recurrence is common.

## Simplified explanation

This is **pityriasis versicolor** caused by *Malassezia*; confirm it with a **Wood's lamp** and a **KOH scraping**.

body:
A 50-year-old HIV-positive male presents to the emergency room with a two-day history of fever and haemoptysis. Chest radiograph shows a fibrocavitary lesion in the right middle lobe. Biopsy of the afflicted area demonstrates septate hyphae that branch at acute angles.

Describe the pathogenesis of his infection.
answer:
The agent is ***Aspergillus*** (usually *A. fumigatus*) — **septate hyphae branching at acute (≈45°) angles**.

**Pathogenesis**
1. *Aspergillus* conidia are **ubiquitous in the environment** (soil, decaying vegetation, dust, construction work) and are **inhaled** constantly; they are small enough to reach the alveoli.
2. In a healthy host, mucociliary clearance and **alveolar macrophages** destroy conidia, and **neutrophils** kill any hyphae that form.
3. In this patient, **impaired immunity** (advanced HIV, and especially neutropenia, steroids or pre-existing lung damage) allows conidia to **germinate into hyphae**.
4. Hyphae **invade lung tissue** and, characteristically, **blood vessels (angioinvasion)**, causing thrombosis, **infarction and necrosis** — hence haemoptysis and cavitation.
5. Fungal enzymes and toxins (proteases, gliotoxin) aid tissue destruction; from the cavity the infection may **disseminate** haematogenously to brain, kidney and other organs.
6. A pre-existing cavity may instead be colonised to form an **aspergilloma (fungus ball)**, and hypersensitivity to the organism causes ABPA — the spectrum of disease depends on host immunity.

> [!answer]
> Inhaled *Aspergillus* conidia escape macrophage and neutrophil killing in the immunocompromised host, germinate into invasive hyphae, and invade lung tissue and blood vessels, causing necrosis, cavitation and haemoptysis, with possible dissemination.
hint: The branching angle and septation name the fungus.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Diagnosis uses histology and culture, plus **galactomannan** and β-D-glucan antigen tests and CT signs (halo and air-crescent). Treatment of choice is **voriconazole** (alternatives: liposomal amphotericin B, isavuconazole), with reversal of immunosuppression where possible.

## Simplified explanation

He has **invasive aspergillosis**: breathed-in spores grew into the lung because his immunity is weak, and the fungus invaded blood vessels, killing tissue and causing bleeding.
